title: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor
description: Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor. "I am putting myself forward to be the Co
body: Conservative MP Sir James Cleverly has said he is resigning from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor. "I am putting myself forward to be the Conservative candidate for mayor of London, because our capital needs more than an administrator," he wrote in the Times, external.Sir James said he has told Tory leader Kemi Badenoch he is stepping down as shadow housing secretary, saying: "I must be free to speak about every aspect of London's future and concentrate fully on winning this race."The capital is not set to vote on a new mayor until May 2028. Labour incumbent Sir Sadiq Khan is yet to confirm whether he will seek an unprecedented fourth term.The Conservatives are yet to pick their candidate for the London mayoral race. A source close to Badenoch said Cleverly "is a formidable politician and will out-campaign Khan".Sir James, who was foreign secretary under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, wrote that he intended to make London a city to be proud of again. "We must rebuild its reputation and make it, once again, the best place in the world to live, work, invest and build a business," he added. A senior Conservative politician, Sir James has held a number of ministerial positions under three prime ministers - including roles as home secretary and education secretary. The army reservist represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015. After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative party leader in 2024, losing out to Badenoch. Reacting to Sir James's announcement, a source said Badenoch "really didn't want James to leave shadow cabinet", but believed "he will be a big asset in London". Current London Mayor Sir Sadiq began his first term in 2016. Cleverly wrote that the capital has been "let down by Labour". He accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of treating London as a "cash cow: somewhere to tax, regulate, raid and blame". Sir James said: "Londoners need homes they can afford to buy or rent. Entrepreneurs need to be able to start and grow businesses without being strangled by cost and regulation."The last time Londoners voted for their mayor in May 2024, Sir Sadiq beat Conservative rival Susan Hall by more than 275,000 votes - representing a swing of 3.2% to Labour.The mayor won nine of the 14 constituencies including two gains from the Tories, and gained 43.8% of the vote share. Reform UK revealed its candidate for the May 2028 election in January when it announced Westminster City councillor Laila Cunningham would be standing.Reacting on social media, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage wrote the Conservatives are "done for", and said Cleverly "will not be the first Tory MP to give up any hope of winning their seat in Essex". Cleverly has not resigned as an MP yet.His announcement follows speculation in recent weeks that he would step down and launch a bid to become London's next mayor.During his time at the London Assembly, Cleverly chaired the London Fire and Emergency Planning Authority, and also worked for Boris Johnson while he was mayor of London.

schema.headline: Cleverly quits shadow cabinet to run for London mayor

title: Norway's Haakon remembers 'my dear father' in first speech as king
description: Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal valu
body: Haakon stressed national unity in the speech, saying the royal family believed in a "society built on law and justice, where everyone is of equal value".    He said Harald had been a good father to himself and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, as well as a "warm and funny grandfather" to his six grandchildren and a "loving and caring husband" to his widow, Queen Sonja.The new king appeared to choke back tears as he noted that Saturday would have been their 58th wedding anniversary.Harald brought the family together "with a natural authority", of which he might not have been aware himself, his son recalled.He had "always stayed true" to his "values and commitments", the new king stressed."He constantly reminded us in the family that each of us must do things in our own way. Find our own style. Be ourselves," Haakon said.He also remarked on the "powerful and moving experience" of seeing thousands of Norwegians gather outside the royal palace in the capital Oslo with "flowers, tributes and candles"."We are in mourning, yet at the same time it brings comfort and strength that so many are grieving together with us," he said.Norwegians have been laying flowers outside the royal palace in Oslo since news broke that Harald had died on Friday. A national period of mourning has been declared, with no date yet given for his funeral.Among them was Norway's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, who laid flowers outside the palace and signed a book of condolences after greeting the new king, said the country was "united in grief and gratitude".Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in parliament on Tuesday and will later participate in a consecration service with his wife, Queen Mette-Marit - a stripped-down version of a coronation, which Norway no longer holds.He assumes his new role at a difficult time, as the royal family has faced health challenges and scandals this year.Mette-Marit came under scrutiny when it was revealed that she had had a three-year friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, for which she publicly apologised.She later received a lung transplant, after suffering from pulmonary fibrosis since 2018. Doctors will not declare her stable until next year, meaning her husband must balance his new official duties with her care.Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted in June of rape and other offences and sentenced to four years in prison. He is appealing.Høiby is not a member of the royal family, but was raised with them since he was four years old, when Haakon married his mother.Haakon's sister, Märtha Louise, has also courted controversy for remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024, their business activities ultimately leading her to step back from royal duties.Without directly referencing these controversies, Haakon said during his speech: "Our family has experienced the importance of standing together in order to remain steadfast both within ourselves and for one another even during difficult times."He said he, along with Mette-Marit and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, would "always strive to understand the life situations of different people".He added: "No one who lives in this country knows what we will face together, but what we do know is that we will stand by one another through both good days and difficult ones."Although Harald remained popular until his death, a poll for newspaper Aftenposten earlier this year suggested that support for the monarchy had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.However, Norwegian royal experts told the BBC that the new king, while facing questions about the turbulence surrounding his family, was respected, hard-working and, they believed, able to move forward despite the challenges.

schema.headline: Norway's Haakon remembers 'my dear father' in first speech as king

title: Croatian refugee tracks down Mold siblings who sent him a gift 33 years ago
description: A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more
body: A man forced to flee war in Croatia as a child has used social media to find and thank the siblings from Wales, who sent him a Christmas present more than 30 years ago.Dalibor Sentic was 10 when in the early 1990s his family fled the newly independent country - which had recently become involved in the Balkan war - for Stockholm, Sweden.Dalibor had received a gift from two young siblings, eight-year-old Claire and Peter, six, from Mold, Flintshire, and had hoped to track them down but only had limited information on them.Decades later, Dalibor, now 44, was able to find the pair to thank them, saying the gesture had "meant a lot" at a time of great difficulty.Describing fleeing his homeland as a child, Dalibor said "we had basically nothing"."It was like starting all over again."I was so innocent but remember hearing the bombs," he said.Dalibor said that, despite the conflict surrounding them, his parents made sure he felt "loved and secure", although he added that moving countries was "tough on a kid". Some months before they fled, Dalibor said his teacher took him into a room full of packages, telling him to choose one to open.It contained a picture of Claire and Peter, which he held onto for more than three decades. "The older you get the more you understand the meaning behind small gestures... it meant a lot," he said.

schema.headline: Croatian refugee tracks down Mold siblings who sent him a gift 33 years ago

title: Cody Gakpo transfer news: Manchester City open talks with Liverpool
description: Liverpool view Gakpo as a proven multi-functional Premier League attacker and he has shown that with a goal and an assist in their first two games thi
body: Liverpool view Gakpo as a proven multi-functional Premier League attacker and he has shown that with a goal and an assist in their first two games this season.But all summer, the understanding has been that if the club bring in the attacking players they want, they would not stand in the way of Gakpo if a solid offer came in. Given how late in the transfer window the talks are taking place between Liverpool and Manchester City, the Anfield side will now consider the situation before sanctioning any move. Liverpool are also hoping to bring in another winger before deadline day.With the arrival of Victor Munoz, the emergence of Rio Ngumoha and Barcola's imminent move from PSG, Gakpo is well aware that he may not be first choice any more, so if a move does happen it would not come as a surprise.Financially it will be a great outcome for Liverpool if they agree a deal for about £85m given they signed Gakpo for £35m from PSV Eindhoven after the World Cup in 2022.But with Hugo Ekitike missing until 2027 with a ruptured Achilles tendon, and Isak's injury struggles, they would be taking a massive risk letting Gakpo leave.

title: 'Keep walking, keep happy': 100-year-old still does a mile a day
description: Image caption, Centenarian Peter Byers enjoys walking and regular fishing tripsByEast Yorkshire and Lincolnshire health and social care correspondentF
body: Image caption, Centenarian Peter Byers enjoys walking and regular fishing tripsByEast Yorkshire and Lincolnshire health and social care correspondentFor 100-year-old Peter Byers, the secret to a long, active life is to "keep happy, keep walking and "keep breathing".The father of five from Pocklington, East Yorkshire, said he walked into town most days "to make sure people know I'm still alive."Peter, who underwent heart surgery five years ago, also enjoys week-long fishing breaks with his son.He said his mobility scooter was gathering dust in the garage, adding: "I go and charge it up regularly like I'm supposed to, but it's never moved."Image source, Family photoImage caption, Peter Byers with his 100th birthday card from the KingPeter said walking helped him "escape the four walls", meet people and, most importantly, "keep my legs going".Five years ago, he had heart surgery at Castle Hill Hospital, near Hull, to treat severe aortic stenosis."It was all explained to me what they were going to do. It's an iffy thing, but I said 'go for it'. And it's done me the world of good."It perked me up. I started to enjoy life again. I started back on American Square dancing and I go out with my children. We do everything together."Asked what his family think of his new lease of life, he laughed and said: "They think I'm a nuisance. I'm keeping saying, 'let's do this, let's do that'."Image source, Family photoImage caption, Peter Byers travelled the world with the Royal Corps of SignalsA patient's age does not need to be a barrier to treatment, according to the cardiology team at Castle Hill.Dr Manish Ramlall, a consultant intervention cardiologist, said: "Mr Byers is a very well man, leading a very active life, and, for him, age is very much just a number."Peter served in the Royal Navy and the Royal Corps of Signals, a career that took him round the world and allowed him to enjoy his passion for fishing as far afield as Malaysia."It's a good life, and you've got to make the best of it," he said. "Keep happy, keep walking."He said he received a card for his 90th birthday that set out the secret to a long and active life."It said 'keep breathing', which I thought was a good idea."

schema.headline: 'Keep walking, keep happy': 100-year-old still does a mile a day

title: David Moyes: Everton manager on fans' anger at potential Harrison Armstrong sale
description: "Supporters aren't always wrong" was David Moyes' reaction to Everton fans voicing their opposition to the potential sale of teenage midfielder Harris
body: "Supporters aren't always wrong" was David Moyes' reaction to Everton fans voicing their opposition to the potential sale of teenage midfielder Harrison Armstrong during the 1-1 draw at Bournemouth. BBC Sport reported earlier on Saturday that Nottingham Forest had put in a £40m bid for the England Under-19 international, who is regarded as one of the brightest prospects to emerge from Finch Farm in recent years.The 19-year-old started at Vitality Stadium as the Toffees rescued a late draw and their travelling supporters repeatedly chanted that there would be "a riot" if Armstrong was sold. "I think you always have to consider supporters; supporters aren't always wrong," said Everton manager Moyes. "But then there are also times where I've had people at clubs who are really powerful and make difficult decisions."I'd bring into that Bryan Gray, who was at Preston North End, and Sir Philip Carter, who was at Everton when I first came in. Not all decisions are popular, and sometimes they have to do it for different reasons."Managers have to make decisions on players sometimes and they feel like huge decisions. But there are sometimes bigger decisions to be made and the club will, I'm sure, make what they think is the right one."If I'd say something to them (the fans), I'd say their manager's an Evertonian."Armstrong has made 24 appearances for Everton and played 87 minutes against the Cherries before he was replaced by Charly Alcaraz. Moyes has been frustrated by the club's lack of signings and he made it clear he wanted reinforcements after the Carabao Cup second-round win against Preston on Wednesday. The Toffees have been searching for a replacement for right-back Seamus Coleman for more than a year. Moyes stressed any decision about Armstrong's future would ultimately rest with Everton, owned by The Friedkin Group. "It's not really a question for just now. It will be a club decision," he said. Speaking to Sky Sports, the Scot also questioned whether the summer transfer window should remain open once the season has started."For all the years I've been in the Premier League this is probably the first time I've thought it was really a nonsense we're still playing games when the window is still open," said Moyes, who is in the final year of his Everton contract. "It feels like we'd have been better off just getting it shut."Maybe it's just the way I am at the moment, I might feel better on Tuesday, but just at the moment it just leaves too much open, too much talk, mainly from the media."If I look back over the years, back to Wayne Rooney, Mikel Arteta, Joleon Lescott, players at Everton I didn't want to lose, more recently Declan Rice at West Ham, sometimes it's part of the journey and you have to rebuild." The window for the Premier League and EFL clubs to make new signings is to close on Tuesday, 1 September at 23:00 BST. The Friedkin Group (TFG), Everton's American owners, will be risking the fury of their own fanbase should they agree to the sale of Armstrong to Nottingham Forest.The notion that Everton could even consider parting with Armstrong sparked an instant reaction of disbelief and anger among supporters, with the teenager regarded as their brightest home-grown prospect for years and a big hope for the future.As yet, there are no indications that Everton will accept an offer, but Forest's interest is real, although it would be a real coup should they pull it off.It would also send out worrying signals about the scale of TFG's ambitions.Manager Moyes has been frustrated by the club's lack of incoming transfer activity this summer.Moyes made it abundantly clear after Wednesday's 4-0 win at Championship side Preston in the Carabao Cup that he wanted reinforcements.His hope was that TFG would provide backing for further arrivals.Since then, however, Everton's main creator Iliman Ndiaye has been heavily linked with Manchester City, and now Forest are ready to test their resolve over Armstrong.How Moyes would view, or indeed explain, such a sale, would be intriguing. It would appear totally at odds with his stated intention of building a better squad.And while Everton and their support may have to accept their prize assets being spirited away by clubs such as Manchester City, the idea that their most promising young player could be taken away by Nottingham Forest – a club they would be expecting to challenge or even surpass – may be harder to stomach.That is why the manner in which Everton handle Forest's approach for Armstrong, who has already excelled this season, may be a defining moment for TFG and Moyes.

schema.headline: David Moyes: Everton manager on fans' anger at potential Harrison Armstrong sale

title: Nepal flood devastation revealed in satellite imagery
description: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.Satellite images also show the formation of a barrie
body: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The BBC spoke to parents and experts to find out their back-to-school tipsByEmily HoltIt's back-to-school tim
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The BBC spoke to parents and experts to find out their back-to-school tipsByEmily HoltIt's back-to-school time again - and families brace for the challenge of swapping summer lie-ins for school routines, easing first-day nerves and getting ready for the year ahead.While children in Scotland returned to school in mid-August, children in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will be returning in the coming week as September begins. We spoke to experts to find out their six key tips to make going back to school as stress-free as possible. Keep a consistent morning routine Cerys Parker, a teacher and blogger, says one of the best ways to keep organised during school time is to keep a consistent morning routine. Her morning starts 30 minutes before her children wake up, for some alone time and a hot coffee.She  then makes them the same breakfast every morning, which they eat together with no screens, then it's upstairs for showers and getting ready for school. Image source, Cerys ParkerImage caption, Parker also keeps copies of her children's timetables so she knows what to prepare on specific days, such as when they have PEShe grabs their lunch boxes and they leave the house at 07:30 for the bus, or 07:50 if Parker is dropping them at school on the way to her own job.The night before, she makes sure school bags are packed, shoes are ready, uniform is laid out and lunch is packed for the morning. "We have things in the same place, so the bags are always in the same location, the keys, and that makes the morning smoother. There's no panic about where everything's going to be."Keep a calendar and plan for important days in the school year It is easy to forget non-uniform days, sports days or study sessions.  Parker recommends having a family calendar pinned to your wall or your fridge - somewhere you can easily see it every day. "It's an academic year calendar with a space for each of us, and then an events section, so as soon as a notice comes in, I write it down."This could include things like meal plans, after-school activities or - depending on your child's age - exams. Image source, Cerys ParkerImage caption, Parker's calendar from June, detailing exams, activities and meal plans for herself and her childrenIt's worth reminding yourself of the school holiday dates, while Parker also notes down key days for her children's school year, such as:Children in Need, on Friday, 13 NovemberWorld Book Day, on Thursday, 4 March 2027Red Nose Day, on Friday, 19 March 2027Earth Day, on Thursday, 22 April 2027She also keeps a small purse of coins throughout the year in case her children need some change for non-uniform days or bake sales. Find out how their day was in a different wayAfter school, many children are tired and are not up for discussion about their day, so Will Shield, professor of child and educational psychology at the University of Exeter, suggests changing your approach to the conversation. "Ask some open questions, instead of interrogating them," he says. "Ask what made you smile today? Or who did you play with at lunchtime?"These sorts of questions are a lot easier to answer for a child, he says, instead of asking what they did. Image caption, Martha Deiros Collado says children getting emotional at the school gates is perfectly normalParker suggests similar questions, like: "What was the silliest thing that happened, or what made you laugh today?"For younger children, clinical psychologist Dr Martha Deiros Collado told CBeebies Parenting Download  that pick-up time should not be a "sign of alarm"."See it as part of the process of separating and loving you, missing you, which is really important."Introduce the idea of school before the big day Many families will have children attending school for the first time, which can be just as big a moment for parents as it is for new pupils.Shield says parents should "reassure themselves" about the routine they will need to follow on school mornings. "Visit the school, walk or drive past it, bring bedtimes back a bit earlier so it's not just a big start in the first week," he says.He also encourages parents to introduce their child into the concept of school, through things like:Reading books about schoolGoing through the school websiteTrying on the new school uniform or PE kitImage source, Will ShieldImage caption, Shield adds that you don't want to overwhelm your child with information about school, but get them to a point where it feels "familiar"Deiros Collado says school readiness is not about "numbers and letters". "It's about much more basic things, like feeling comfortable and safe to be in a classroom with other children," she says. Building independence can also help bridge the gap between home and school life, she says, by encouraging your child to do some things by themselves, such as zipping up their own coat. "It's just building that sense of, I'm ready to do this without you," she says. But Deiros Collado also stresses that your child should be able to ask for help when they need it. "One of the best skills you can give your little ones is being able to say to an adult, 'Help me,' because you want your kid to be able to say that to a teacher."She also suggests a "goodbye ritual" with your child to practise separation, such as blowing a kiss. Image source, Katharine RadiceImage caption, Katharine Radice says that focusing too much on the homework outcome you want for your child can be "demotivating" for them Katharine Radice, teacher and author, recommends putting together a homework timetable. "Doing this puts boundaries around homework and makes it easier to ring-fence distraction-free time," she says.This could be different every week depending on different activities, but Radice stresses there should be a plan in advance so it's not left to the last minute.For supporting children with homework, Radice suggests approaching the task in a "positive and open way" and listening to what they might be finding difficult. She also recommends looking for opportunities to praise your child's effort in doing work to help them "stay motivated." "If your child thinks their outcomes won't meet your expectations, they may start to feel that their effort is pointless," she says. Don't just reassure children - listen to themSome children who are returning to school may have anxieties about the year ahead, and Shield recommends to sit with your child and listen to their concerns."Don't immediately reassure them by saying, 'You'll be fine,'" he says."The child's got no evidence they will be fine because they're worried."He suggests phrases such as "I can see you're worried" to make a child feel listened to. It is also worth trying to dig deeper to find out what is making them worried about school specifically. He also recommends some gentle encouragement of positive things they like about school to ease some worries, such as lunchtime or playing sports with friends. If anxiety does become overwhelming for them, if they aren't sleeping or it is stopping them from doing everyday things, then Shield recommends talking to the school or a local GP.

schema.headline: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier

title: Frinton Normandy veteran who lied about age to enlist dies
description: The charity's vice president, Dick Goodwin, said: "Don was incredibly special."He had a warmth and presence that lit up every room he entered, and he
body: The charity's vice president, Dick Goodwin, said: "Don was incredibly special."He had a warmth and presence that lit up every room he entered, and he touched the lives of so many people."As a World War Two veteran, Don represented a generation whose courage and service we will never forget. "It was a privilege for the taxi charity to know him, and he will be remembered with enormous affection and gratitude. "My thoughts are with his family and all those who loved him at this very sad time."In an interview last year, Turrell said: "I did lie about my age. I pushed it up a bit, gave all the right answers, and I was in. I was happy."He explained he had always wanted to be a soldier and that like "all the young lads" he had wanted to play his part in defending his country.The veteran described feeling "excited and apprehensive" during the crossing to the Normandy coast, and said his "introduction" to the war was seeing bodies from earlier fighting washing back up on the beach as he landed.His war came to an end a few weeks later on July 10, when he was seriously injured during fighting near the town of Eterville. He was later medically discharged.Turrell spoke movingly of the close friends he lost during the campaign, some of whom he buried in the field, and who are now buried in Commonwealth war cemeteries on the continent. The war also claimed his older brother Leslie, who had been a telegraphist on HMS Penelope and died when she was sunk off the Italian coast near Naples in February 1944.Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below.

title: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal
description: Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.The brother of
body: Families are flying out to Nepal to help the ongoing search for 33 British nationals still missing after deadly floods hit the country.The brother of Neetu Goyal Tiwari, one of the missing Brits who has not been seen since Wednesday, has appealed to officials to locate his sister."Please help us find her", Naresh Goyal told the BBC as he struggled to hold back his emotions.On Friday, Nepalese authorities named 573 tourists who are still missing in the country and despite fears of a second wave of flooding, search efforts have continued.To help, the UK is deploying a rapid deployment team to Nepal to support British nationals affected in the region. The specially-trained crisis response team is expected to arrive in Kathmandu on Saturday, a move that follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge of £5m worth of humanitarian support for relief and recovery efforts. And as rescue efforts continue in the aftermath of the disaster which killed at least 538 people, details of the missing are slowly emerging.Tiwari, 51, had travelled to Nepal to take part in the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrimage, which was "her dream", her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC.She travelled to Delhi from London before heading to Kathmandu on 14 August with a group from the spiritual organisation Isha Foundation.Tiwari was expected to return to India on Thursday and meet her brother and parents. But now, the family is desperately searching for answers."We have called every helpline given by the Indian government and reached out to the British Embassy in Kathmandu as well," Goyal said."Please help us find her," he said, his voice breaking. "We are all very scared."Neetu's husband, Shantanu, added she had been at the Gyirong checkpoint when the floods struck, so the search for her is being coordinated by China. Anant Patel told BBC Your Voice that he is still waiting for news on his missing parents, Bipin and Mala Patel, who are from Coventry. The 29-year-old believes his parents - who are also on a pilgrimage - crossed into Tibet from Nepal moments before the landslide hit the Gyirong border crossing.He and his brother Deepesh are in touch with the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and he told the BBC: "It's a difficult situation for us all, and we are doing our best to stay strong as best as we can in the circumstances."Pramod Poudel, who lives in Uckfield in East Sussex, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife Sumitra Sapkota and family since the flood hit on Wednesday."It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said.Poudel, who goes by the name Pedro, said he is travelling home to Nepal because "my family needs me".The daughter of Hemangini Patel, 65, said she is still yet to hear from her mother or her aunt Hema Amin, 63.Patel told BBC Your Voice her mother's last known location is from a TikTok video shared at 06:00 Nepal time, crossing into Tibet.She said her mother and aunt had been travelling with the Alpine Eco Trek tour when the flooding hit."We are trying to get through to British embassy in China but can't even get through," Patel said.Essex nurse Rajendra Pudasaini said his relatives were "swept away" by the floods."My wife's auntie and uncle, and their granddaughter and her husband are missing, and my godson as well," he said. "They're gone. The speed the water came, they couldn't be saved, they were just swept away."Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he hasn't heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, and sister-in-law Ankita Chandra, 35.He said he'd last heard from Ankit on 26 August when he had been travelling with tour operator Kailash Journey on a pilgrimage.The whole group is now missing, Ranjan said, adding: "We don't know if they crossed the border... We don't have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated." Also missing is Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse at Darent Valley Hospital in Kent. Her brother Shambhu said that her family was desperately waiting for news of her safety after she lost contact with her relatives while on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash. "My dear sister, wherever you are, please stay strong. We are praying for your safety every moment and waiting desperately for you to return home," he wrote on social media.A family of four, including an 18-year-old A-Level student and a 13-year-old girl, from Surrey are also among the missing. Spandan Sahu, 18, was in Nepal with his father Santosh Sahu, 46, his mother Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44, and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.Spandan had just finished his A-levels at Royal Grammar School Guildford.In a statement, a spokesperson for the school said: "It is with great concern that we have been informed that a former student, along with members of his family, have been reported missing in Nepal."Whilst we are hoping for positive news, we do not have any further information at this time."Our thoughts, love and deepest sympathies are with all of the families and loved ones of anyone affected by this tragedy in Nepal at this incredibly difficult time."Vikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he has not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy, since the flooding hit. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit. "We're not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week," Kolagatla added."The kids still don't believe it. They think she's stuck in the flood and that she'll come back. They think she's stuck somewhere and there's no mobile network."Prajval Haldia can remember dropping his parents Pavan Haldia and Kavita Haldia off at the airport for their trip to Kathmandu, spending a few days sightseeing before moving on to Mount Kailash.He spoke to the BBC from the south London Sanatan Mandir temple, where 16 people from the community have been missing since Wednesday."Everyone here is in the same position and that's really helping," he told the BBC. "I'm just trying to stay positive, no news is good news sometimes, I guess.""Obviously it's a very difficult time. There's ups and downs when you think about certain things, but we're just hoping and really praying that everything's ok and they are going to be back soon," he says.Elsewhere, Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, from Slough, was among 27 travellers linked to the tour company who remain unaccounted for.Her husband, Bhupesh Bector, told The Times: "I know that she's in Nepal for sure, so even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there."University of Kent graduate Nabhi Das from Streatham in South London has also been widely reported as missing Nepal.A British psychiatrist is also among the missing.Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims in Tibet when the floods hit, the Telegraph reports.His wife, Manjula Atmakur, has travelled to Nepal to help look for him.She said she felt let down by the British government's response to the flooding.Several of those missing had been making a pilgrimage to the sacred Hindu site of Mount Kailash, Nepalese tour operator The Trekkers' Society said.The operator said nine British nationals on one of its tours to the site were among those unaccounted for, including four males, aged 14, 50, 50 and 54, and five females, aged 40, 46, 50, 50 and 53.Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.

schema.headline: What we know about the 33 British nationals missing in Nepal

title: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls
description: Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.Sussex Police said i
body: Organisers of a Christian festival say they are "devastated" after a man died and six other people were injured by a falling sign.Sussex Police said it had been called to the Big Church Festival at Wiston Park, near Steyning in West Sussex, at about 15:38 BST on Friday.It was later confirmed a 41-year-old man from Eastbourne in East Sussex had died.The Archbishop of Canterbury said she was "sad and shocked" to hear about the fatal incident.Dame Sarah Mullally said: "I pray for his family, friends and loved ones as they grieve. I pray for those receiving treatment, and the healthcare workers looking after them."And I pray too for the other festival goers, staff and event organisers as they come to terms with these tragic events. "May the God of comfort and healing be with them all."South East Coast Ambulance service said four of the six people injured were taken to local hospitals for further treatment, with two people having serious injuries.The Big Church Festival, which describes itself as the UK's biggest Christian festival, was founded in 2009.The festival began on Friday and was due to continue until Sunday, but a decision was made by organisers to cancel the remainder of the event after the incident."We are working with the emergency services, police and the Health and Safety Executive as they establish the circumstances surrounding today's incident," the organisers said."We are incredibly grateful to everyone who responded, and to our teams and community for the care they have shown one another."

schema.headline: Big Church Festival 'devastated' as man dies after sign falls

title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK shortly, source tells BBC
description: Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.It is believed sh
body: Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported, external.It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.In one email exchange from 2011, she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family." A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

schema.headline: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK shortly, source tells BBC

title: I was told I was unworthy to be a mother. Then they stole my baby
description: Figure caption, Maron only had a few months to get to know her baby before he was taken from herByNichola RutherfordBBC Scotland NewsMarion McMillan w
body: Figure caption, Maron only had a few months to get to know her baby before he was taken from herByNichola RutherfordBBC Scotland NewsMarion McMillan was 17, pregnant and unmarried, when she made her first trip to England from her home in the south-west of Scotland. It was 1966 and she was sent by her family to a maternity home run by the Salvation Army more than 150 miles away, in Newcastle-upon-Tyne.The young mum spent nine months with her baby - a beautiful boy with "gorgeous wee black hair" - before he was taken from her. She begged staff to let her keep him. "I said 'please help me keep my baby, don't let them take my baby, please' and he was gone," she told a new BBC documentary, Stolen Babies.Warning: This story contains racist language and descriptions of sexual abuse and violenceIt tells the stories of some of the 250,000 women who were forced to hand over their newborns for adoption between 1949 and 1976.They were powerless against the will of the state, social workers and religious organisations, and the system which supplied infants to adoptive families. "Let's face it, we were working class unmarried girls having babies that were being adopted by middle class women," another victim, Ann Keen, told the programme. For years many of the women kept their ordeal - their shame - secret. In July, outgoing prime minister Sir Keir Starmer issued a formal apology to those mothers, telling them: "The shame is not yours... the shame is ours."Marion's story: 'They cannae take my baby away from me'Image source, Marion McMillanImage caption, Marion fell in love with a refugee from Pakistan when she was 17Marion grew up in Stranraer in the 1960s where she fell for an older man who had emigrated from Pakistan. "I was in love at the time and it was so lovely, I never gave it a second thought," she said."We were only together just a few short times, and I'd never told my family but at 17 I became pregnant out of wedlock."She hoped they would marry but her boyfriend knew their relationship would not be accepted. "Nobody will want you to go with a black man, Marion," he told her. In their last conversation, he suggested emigrating to Hawaii where he believed mixed-race marriages were more acceptable. "I never saw him ever again after that," she said. "Didn't know what was ahead of me. The conveyor belt of 'unwed mother' took control, and that was when I lost control."Image source, Marion McMillanImage caption, Marion McMillan said her son was born with a beautiful head of dark hairShe gave birth at Hopedene, a home for unmarried mothers where conditions were austere and treatment could be brutal. "Everything, from the minute you cross their threshold, is that you're unworthy to be a mother and we're taking your baby from you," Marion said. "It's going for adoption. So you better get used to that, girl, because you've no money, you've no place to live, you've not got anybody to support you." While giving birth she was slapped across the face by the matron for trying to get off a bed. "And I don't know what was worse, the shock of her doing that [or] being in heavy labour," she said.  "And the next thing my son is born."She wasn't allowed to hold him until the following day. "I was absolutely terrified," Marion said. "Absolutely terrified that they're taking my baby. They cannae take my baby away from me."Image source, Marion McMillanImage caption, Her son was taken from her when he was just nine months oldBut Marion got to spend longer with her baby than some of the other girls in mother and baby homes across the UK. "I was a Scotch girl with a half-caste, that's what the Salvation Army recognised me to be," Marion said. "And of course you were told that half-caste is very rarely successful in adoption."He was nine months old when he was picked out by his adoptive parents. Marion compared the wait to hand him over to death row. "[The matron] took him, and she was weeping with me, and she must have had another member of staff that took him then, and she was still holding me."Her desperate pleas to keep the baby were ignored. Image source, Finestripe ProductionsImage caption, Marion was finally reunited with her son in 2004. Unwelcome back home in Stranraer, she ended up in a women's hostel in Glasgow. "Suddenly I'm banished from where I was born and brought up and I'm entirely on my own again," she told BBC Scotland News. Marion was finally reunited with her son in 2004, but her experience as a teenager continues to cast a long shadow. "It's been painful for him, painful for me, painful for his [adoptive] parents, painful for everybody. "But it you take away the pain it's been a gift from God because all the years I missed him."Stolen BabiesThe full scale of the UK's forced adoption scandal, as told by the mothers and children separated from one anotherWatch on BBC Scotland at 21:00 on Tuesday and afterwards on BBC iPlayer. Ann Keen: 'I was told I'd never see him again'Image source, Ann KeenImage caption, Ann Keen was refused pain relief during labour - an "awful ordeal"Ann Keen was 17 and working in a toilet roll factory in Ewloe, Flintshire, when she was asked out by a handsome salesman. "That's when it happened. In today's terms it was without consent. You didn't say that in the 60s," she said.Like Marion, she was sent away so the problem could be "dealt with". She gave birth at an NHS hospital in Swansea, where she was denied pain relief. "I was told I wouldn't have anything for pain because I would remember it, and I wouldn't be a bad girl again," she said."They saw me as a woman that didn't have any morality and therefore I wasn't worthy of any help.  And I don't believe, had I been married that that would have happened."Image source, Ann KeenImage caption, Ann's son was taken away when he was just eight days old. Ann was told that she could spend 10 days with her baby but on the eighth day she went to the nursery and he wasn't there. A "cruel" midwife told her: "He's waiting for his new mummy. You'll never see him again."She took her to a Victorian bathroom, put her in the bath and grabbed her breast. The midwife told Ann: "I'm getting rid of this milk, you won't be needing it.""And that's when I knew I'd lost everything," Ann said. Joan Chambers: 'Teachers are supposed to be trustworthy'Image source, Joan ChambersImage caption, Joan became pregnant when she 14Joan Chambers was a 14-year-old schoolgirl in Sunderland when she realised she was pregnant. A teacher had starting asking her to go for walks in the countryside."I wasn't alarmed by it, because, you know, he was a teacher and teachers are supposed to be trustworthy. I trusted him, I really did."One day he raped her. "All I remember is the pain," she said. "I didn't understand what was happening."Five weeks before giving birth, she had to give evidence against the man in court. Years later she discovered archives that showed that the judge had told the jury not to believe her testimony. She told the documentary that the judge said: "He's got a good career ahead of him, so don't let her being pregnant sway you."She went on: "That hurt. It really hurt when I read that years later. For a judge to say that."The man was acquitted.Image source, Finestripe ProductionsImage caption, Years later Joan discovered the jury had been told not to believe her evidenceJoan spent the last few weeks of her pregancy at a mother and baby home - but she said she had "blanked out" the birth. "It must have been so painful. I wasn't given painkillers or anything like that, " she added. "The next thing I remember is like my legs were up in stirrups, a green cover over my legs, waiting for the doctor to come and stitch me. I had been torn to shreds, absolutely torn to shreds."Her baby was taken when he was three weeks old, a week before Christmas. "They took him from me and then they told me to go back in the nursery and take the bedding out of his cot and get it ready for the next baby," she said. Joan was 66 when they were finally reunited. "It was amazing, but it was so sad," she said. "He'd never looked for me because he had a happy adoption."'The apologies prove we weren't to blame'In 2023, Nicola Sturgeon described Marion McMillan as "one of the most ardent campaigners" as she formally apologised for the role of the state in the forced adoptions."It was always cruel, unjust and profoundly wrong," Scotland's first minister said. In an updated apology , externalpublished on Friday, The Salvation Army said it was "profoundly sorry and deeply ashamed" that vulnerable young women did not get the help they needed in their mother and baby homes. "We know we must be held accountable for those we let down and reflect on our role in a society that worked against pregnant unmarried women," its territorial leaders, commissioners Paul and Jenine Main, added. Marion says still more can be done. She wants more support for the victims of forced adoption - mothers, children and adoptive parents.And she would like to see a centre of excellence for adoption in Scotland, where anyone involved in adoption can receive comprehensive training and support. Image source, Finestripe ProductionsImage caption, Ann was reunited with her son, Mark Lloyd-Fox, in later lifeAnn Keen was among a small group of mothers invited to Downing Street ahead of Starmer's apology on behalf of the UK government. "The apology to me means I'm no longer presumed guilty of something I didn't do, because I didn't give him away. He was taken," she said. "It will prove to the world that it wasn't our fault. We weren't to blame. The state was to blame, the churches were to blame, and we will be free."If you or someone you know has been affected by sexual abuse or violence, you can find details of organisations that can help at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: I was told I was unworthy to be a mother. Then they stole my baby

title: England v Pakistan: Nasser Hussain calls early end to play at Lord's 'a joke'
description: The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nas
body: The decision to abandon play an hour before scheduled at the end of the third day of England's second Test against Pakistan was called "a joke" by Nasser Hussain.On a Saturday badly affected by persistent showers at Lord's, players left the field at 17:08 BST.At that point, prospects of conditions improving sufficiently for play to resume seemed remote. However, rain cleared and the sky brightened.The groundstaff partially removed the covers while officials deliberated. At 18:30, with up to an hour of playing time remaining and with the weather the best it had been all day, umpires Paul Reiffel and Allahuddien Parker abandoned proceedings.The decision was greeted with booing by some of the sparse crowd that remained inside the ground."That's a joke, honestly a joke," former England captain Hussain said on Sky Sports."I earlier said how good the umpires have been. These fans have waited all afternoon for it to stop raining. It's now bright. There's blue sky in the distance. That is an unbelievable decision, it really is."In about five minutes' time it's going to be sunny here."The weather stayed dry and the light remained good up to 19:30, the time at which play would have been scheduled to close.The morning session had been washed out and only 24.5 overs of play were possible as the players dodged the showers, meaning spectators will receive a 50% refund on the price of their ticket.If 30 overs had been completed, spectators would not have been entitled to any money back.Still, the abandonment caused some fans to express their displeasure with messages to the BBC's live coverage of the Test."Sat in the Edrich Stand," wrote Joe at Lord's. "It hasn't rained for half an hour and it's as bright as it's been all day. Absolutely no justification for not playing right now. A real shame."Rachel in Kingswinford added: "Ridiculous to call it off! They want fans supporting Test cricket and those spectators have stuck with it all day - another 30-45 mins of play would have been a better look (plus saving authorities money on refunds)!"Another message from Paul in Northwich read: "This is a terrible advert for cricket. It's like the umpires are waiting for it to rain again. At least the spectators can get a refund."Play ended with England 177-7 in their second innings, 357 ahead and on course to win the match and series.Batting conditions had been difficult all day and it would have been another challenging period for the home side had they been asked to return for a short time late in the evening."It would have been a tricky 40 minutes to go out there and bat," said Dan Lawrence, who made an unbeaten 50."It's nice to have a good sleep and think about how I'm going to play in the morning. I can imagine it will be with the same intent and trying to push the game forward."Forty minutes of batting at 6.45pm is never an ideal thing."The situation at Lord's came on the same day Durham were denied the chance to chase a victory target of four against Gloucestershire because of bad light at the end of the third day of their County Championship match at Chester-le-Street.It means the teams will return on Sunday for what could be as little as one ball of action.Gloucestershire were dismissed for 250 in their second innings in the closing stages of Saturday, with visiting coach Mark Alleyne claiming the light was already too poor before his team were all out."I'm not sure where to start, really," said Alleyne. "I mean, 45 minutes before we lost the last wicket, it was too dark to play, which would have been consistent with all the other days that we played.""We had probably 50 minutes of cricket there that we probably shouldn't have done."The match could have been concluded had Gloucestershire chosen to bowl spin, only for the away side to refuse and push the game into a Sunday when rain is forecast."They asked if we would bowl our spinners to finish the game," added Alleyne. "Of course, we said no, we'll bowl our quick bowlers, in which case it became bad light, so we'll come back tomorrow."Durham coach Ryan Campbell wrote on X: "Cricket sometimes doesn't help itself. Before everyone loads up on the poor old umpires, it's not their fault."

schema.headline: England v Pakistan: Nasser Hussain calls early end to play at Lord's 'a joke'
